title: Leo Watson and the Spirits of Rhythm
summary: Dickenson recorded with Leo Watson, a trombonist who mainly sang and kept him laughing; Morgenstern praises his As Long As I Live.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: There's another guy, Skip Mancrullers (PHONETIC) too. He's all right. I think he's with Leo Watson's band.
Well you recorded with him.
Yeah. I recorded (inaudible).
I heard you say was that Leo was quite a trombone player too.
He was a trombone player.
But he never really -- he never really featured at --
No, singing -- that was his main thing. I forget what band he was with -- it was some big band.
Krupa --
Or was it Jan Taylor?
He was with Gene Krupa for awhile.
Was it Gene Krupa?
Yeah.
I thought it was Jan Stafford or something like that.
That was -- Bon Bon was with Jan Stafford.
Oh yeah, Bon Bon. But didn't Bon Bon follow Herring (PHONETIC) or something?
Could be. Maybe he -- it might have been. He probably never made any records cause he made some records with Gene -- "Nagasaki," which is pretty wild.
Yeah, he was a pretty wild guy. He'd keep you laughing.
Yeah.
Every time I had to work with him I had to laugh all the time I was playing. He was funny.
But he also -- he sang some beautiful musical things but I've got a record of his of "As Long As I Live" with the Spirits of Rhythm.
Oh yeah.

It takes a long -- it takes up a chorus on there. Just a little humming in the background and it's beautifully really. You know you could play that on an instrument and it would be a lovely song. And I play it (inaudible). It sounds like Lester a little bit before -- you
know -- it's 1935 or something. He comes in so nice.
Uh-huh.
